raw_response:
For this prototype, I would put a small parseOptions(String line) adapter around an existing Java option parser. Raw command-line text needs two operations: turn quoted text into argument tokens, then interpret option names and values. The parsers below address the second operation; Ant supplies a useful component for the first. None of the verified parsers alone was established to satisfy the entire raw-string-to-Map requirement.

1. JArgs — best match for a compact, permissively licensed starting point.
https://jargs.sourceforge.net/
Its CmdLineParser supports short and long options, long values with an equals sign, a double-dash terminator, and concatenated boolean short flags. The project describes itself as compact and BSD licensed. Its site dates release 1.0 to 12 April 2005, so this is supported by evidence before the 2 December 2015 cutoff.
https://jargs.sourceforge.net/doc/api/jargs/gnu/CmdLineParser.html
The important limitations are that parse takes String[], returns void, and exposes results through option accessors; your adapter must tokenize the input and construct the desired Map. Its documented concatenated-option behavior rejects a cluster containing an option that requires a value, so do not assume every GNU clustering edge case works. I did not verify the ideal of copying exactly one source file.

2. Apache Commons CLI, particularly the documented 1.3.1 DefaultParser — a practical option-parsing component with dated evidence.
https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-cli/javadocs/api-release/org/apache/commons/cli/DefaultParser.html
The historical API documents short-option bursting and parsing String[] into CommandLine, with a source revision dated 3 May 2015. Public source also shows handling of long options and an end-of-options prefix.
https://github.com/apache/commons-cli/blob/master/src/main/java/org/apache/commons/cli/DefaultParser.java
Use it after tokenization and copy the resulting options into your own map. It is a library with its own result classes, not a verified single-file implementation. The current source is useful corroboration, but current implementation details are not automatically evidence of 2015 behavior.

3. JOpt Simple — especially useful when a map-shaped result matters.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/apidocs/joptsimple/OptionParser.html
Its API explicitly documents -abc clustering, long options with equals-sign values, and -- termination. OptionSet.asMap() provides a standard Map, although its keys are OptionSpec objects and its values are lists, so a Map keyed by your own option names still requires conversion.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/apidocs/joptsimple/OptionSet.html
It also needs already tokenized arguments. The project change log records the map method in version 4.6 and a switch to the MIT license.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/changes.html
The documentation site is dated 27 November 2018. I am therefore retaining this as later evidence, rather than asserting that the exact inspected version and behavior were available by the cutoff; the date-focused search did not establish a dated older release.

4. Apache Ant Commandline.translateCommandline — a complementary raw-string tokenizer.
https://ant.apache.org/manual/api/org/apache/tools/ant/types/Commandline.html
This static method accepts a String and returns String[]. Its public Java source uses separate ordinary, single-quoted, and double-quoted states, preserves spaces inside quoted arguments, and rejects unbalanced quotes.
https://github.com/apache/ant/blob/master/src/main/org/apache/tools/ant/types/Commandline.java
It can supply the input tokens for one of the option parsers above. It is not itself an option parser, and its small quoting grammar should not be presented as a complete Unix shell lexer: the inspected delimiter set contains ordinary spaces and quotes, and does not establish shell escape, tab-separation, expansion, or substitution semantics. The file carries Apache License 2.0. This live source has no verified pre-cutoff version in this run, so its historical availability is unknown.

For the requested example, the adapter should preserve the message as one token before applying the configured option definitions. Keep non-option operands separately, and consider Map<String, List<String>> if repeated options matter. Both choices make it easier to replace the parser later. This is a proposed integration approach, not a tested implementation.

The public GitHub code-search endpoint was blocked. I used code-through-web search and opened public source pages instead; I am not claiming native code-search success. Apache Commons Exec's string-parsing source was also inspected, but its command/executable model and argument re-quoting make it less direct for this adapter. No claim is made that any candidate was deployed or demonstrated useful in this shell.
